Pool: set of open DB connections kept alive by app (or proxy like PgBouncer). Request needs DB → borrows idle connection → runs queries → returns it, still open. Pool empty → caller waits in queue until one frees or timeout fires. Pool also validates/recycles stale connections and caps the total.

Why it helps: opening a connection is expensive (TCP handshake + TLS + auth + server-side session setup; in Postgres, a whole forked process, several MB each). Per-request connect → that cost on every request, often longer than the query itself. Reuse → pay once. The cap matters as much: DB has a hard connection limit (`max_connections`) and degrades before reaching it, so the pool turns a traffic spike into queueing in the app instead of a DB overload.

Gotchas: bigger pool ≠ faster. DB throughput peaks at a small multiple of its core count; past that, contention → slower. Total connections = pool size × app instances, easy to blow the DB limit when scaling out (→ external pooler). Leaked connections (never returned) or long transactions holding them → pool exhaustion, looks like a hang. Session state (`SET`, temp tables, advisory locks) leaks between borrowers unless reset, and breaks under transaction-mode pooling.
